newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chips recover most of losses, bonds weaker.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chips recover most of losses, bonds weaker.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks rebounded from a big sell-off to end modestly lower Wednesday as investors stepped in to pick up bargains late in the session.
Bonds ended moderately weaker, while the dollar was mixed.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 19.75 points at 6,422.94 after shaking off a loss of more than 75 points.
The rebound came one day after the index of 30 blue-chip stocks dropped 79 points due to heavy profit-taking.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,426 to 1,041 on active volume of 493 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index, however, snapped its seven straight sessions of record closes, ending off 3.35 points at 1,297.02.
Analysts were impressed with the Dow's rebound.
"The sell-off is over," said James Cramer, president of Cramer Co. "We had an unbelievable comeback and buyers came out of the woodwork..."
Smaller-name stocks continued to outperform larger companies.
"It's part of the move from big cap names which have had such a dramatic move," said Jim Pizzo, senior investment strategist at Oppenheimer.

Weighing on stocks during the afternoon was news that Salomon Bros. cut the stock holdings in its recommended portfolio to 45 percent from 50 percent, moving the 5 percent to cash. The allocation is now 20 percent cash, 35 percent bonds and 45 percent stocks.
Salomon's Chief Equity Strategist David Shulman said that based on a "price/sales basis, valuations are the highest in history."
"I see at best a sideways market next year or at worst down 10-15 percent. A correction, not a bear market," he said. "We had two wonderful years so we may have a pause."
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 13/32, raising its yield to 6.40 percent from 6.37 percent at Tuesday's close.

The dollar ended the session modestly higher against the German mark at 1.5605, up from 1.5565 on Tuesday. Against the Japanese yen, the dollar traded in an extremely tight range throughout the day before closing at 113.07 yen, down from 113.37 yen.
Lumber futures jumped again on strong demand and rising prices in the cash market.
Random Lengths, a lumber industry newsletter, quoted cash spruce at $394 for 1,000 board feet Wednesday, up $16 from a week ago. But industry sources said by late Wednesday there were $400 trades.
Lumber for January delivery rose the $10 daily trading limit to $409.30 for 1,000 board feet and March rose $10 to $395.30 at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.

Profit-taking drove gasoline lower. January gasoline fell 0.89 cent to 68.24 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange. January heating oil, pressured by bearish inventory data, lost 0.65 cent to 73.57 cents a gallon. January crude oil fell 13 cents to $24.80 a barrel, pressured by losses in refined products.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index closed down 16.3 points at 4,045.2. In Tokyo, the key Nikkei 225 average inched up 29.35 points or 0.14 percent to finish at 20,659.91.
